extracted.intended_audience: journalism students and newspaper sports writers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing and evaluating newspaper sports (and related feature) stories, including story types, purpose, treatment, style, sourcing, and staffing for big events. Emphasizes accuracy, fairness, writer familiarity with the sport, and narrative techniques for game accounts and analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of sporting news stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Sporting news stories may be divided into three classes: (1) those that deal with the contestants and the conditions before the event, (2) those that report the contest itself, and (3) those that analyze the event and its results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the appropriate class when planning/assigning stories: previews/features (contestants/conditions), straight game reports (play-by-play/firsthand accounts), and post-game analysis (interpretation of results).

rubrics_metrics.name: Source basis for previews and forecasts
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that discuss the relative merits of the contestants and forecast the results of the game are based on first hand observations of the writer or on the observations of others, regarding the showing made by the contestants in previous events and in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground pre-game assessments in direct observation or credible reports of prior performance and practice; avoid speculation unsupported by observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firsthand witnessing for game reports
rubrics_metrics.description: The general and the detailed accounts of a contest can, of course, be written only by writers who have witnessed it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure reporters who write the play-by-play or detailed game account were actually present; secondhand accounts are inappropriate for authentic detailed reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staffing for major events
rubrics_metrics.description: In covering a big sporting event, a newspaper frequently assigns two men to report it, one to write a general account and one a detailed story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For large contests allocate at least two reporters: one to produce a broad, readable general narrative and another to capture detailed, play-by-play or statistics-driven copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writer expertise and familiarity
rubrics_metrics.description: It is evident that all sporting news stories can best be written by men who are thoroughly familiar with the sport itself and with the contestants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign reporters who know the rules, tactics, and personalities of the sport; subject-matter familiarity improves accuracy and the quality of analysis and description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose — serve healthy legitimate interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The general aim of sporting news stories should be to satisfy a normal, healthy interest in legitimate sports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid sensationalizing or unduly promoting harmful aspects (e.g., excessive publicity or prize-fight glorification); consider social effects (such as on schoolboy athletes) when choosing coverage tone and emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy ... is as vital to news stories of sports as to any other news stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify facts, statistics, times, scores, and attributions; accuracy is non-negotiable in all sports reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness / spirit of fair play
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the interest that readers have in local contestants may warrant a writer in devoting considerable space to them, it does not justify him in slighting or treating unfairly their opponents ... The spirit of fair play that is essential to sport is equally necessary to reports of sporting events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid bias toward local teams; provide balanced coverage of both sides and resist partisan exaggeration even when readers favor a local contestant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment and analysis — observation and exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The review of conditions preceding the contest and the analysis of the game and its results require careful observation, clear thinking, and a good expository style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical pieces should combine rigorous observation with logical, clear explanation; adopt expository techniques akin to editorial or critical writing when interpreting results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Game account style — spirited narrative and human interest
rubrics_metrics.description: The account of the event itself demands spirited narrative and description that portrays not only the scenes but the spirit of the occasion. The contrast between the emotions of the victors and those of the vanquished may be used to good advantage. Because of the popular interest in individual players, many events give ample opportunity for developing the personal, or human interest, elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting the contest, use vivid description and narrative pacing to convey drama; incorporate human-interest elements (players' emotions, heroism) without sacrificing accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style — variety, originality, and avoidance of cheap jargon
rubrics_metrics.description: The very popularity of a subject that demands much writing on the same or similar material day by day necessitates variety of presentation. Efforts to avoid constant repetition in reporting baseball games have resulted in some picturesque diction and some original figures of speech in the stories of the clever few, and in much more cheap humor and almost unintelligible jargon in the work of their mediocre imitators. That readable stories can be written in good English with as much originality of style as is to be found in other well written news stories, has been repeatedly demonstrated by a number of writers on sports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for variety and fresh phrasing but avoid cheap humor, meaningless slang or jargon that obscures meaning. Maintain good English and readable prose even when seeking originality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and angle selection (illustrated by eclipse examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: The same facts about the same eclipse are given in different ways (note preceding the two eclipse stories).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose tone and angle appropriate to the audience and purpose: e.g., a solemn 'awe'-filled descriptive approach (Washington Herald) or a lighter, humorous, human-interest approach (Washington Post). Use the same factual elements but vary presentation to suit readers and editorial voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific/technical event reporting — precision and explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: At the Naval Observatory ... observers recorded the first contact of the sun and moon at thirty-five minutes and twenty-eight seconds after 9 o'clock ... Photographs were taken ... The photoheliograph is a photographic camera, forty feet long ... In case of a total eclipse the operation is different ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For reporting scientific or technical phenomena include precise measurements/timings, identify and quote authoritative observers, and explain technical instruments/processes in accessible language so readers understand significance. Provide geographic scope and quantitative detail (percent of sun darkened, where total eclipse occurred) when relevant.
